members.name: tickEnabled
members.doc:
Tick gate — set to false to skip TickComponent without
disabling the component. Cheaper than detaching/reattaching
for things that only sometimes need ticking (e.g. an AI
component that's only active while the player is nearby).

members.name: tickInterval
members.doc:
Tick pacing (UE TickInterval): 0 = every frame. When set, the owning
actor accumulates time and TickComponent fires with the ACCUMULATED
delta once the interval elapses.

members.name: tickGroupOverride
members.doc:
Per-component tick group override. -1 (default) = tick inside the
owner's Tick, in the owner's group. 0..3 = AActor::ETickGroup values
(PrePhysics/DuringPhysics/PostPhysics/PostUpdateWork): the world then
ticks this component in THAT group's pass instead — after every
actor of the group has ticked. An int rather than the enum so this
header keeps its forward-declared AActor.

members.name: AdvanceTickAccumulator
members.doc:
Called by the owning actor's Tick: applies tickInterval pacing.
Returns false to skip this frame; on true, outDelta carries the
accumulated dt to tick with.

types.name: MSaveGame
types.doc:
UE's USaveGame: the player's progress, saved apart from the world. Unlocks,
a crew dossier, the trophy record, settings that follow a profile — what a
world-state slot has no place for, and what must survive a patch that
changes the level. A save object is written to a NAMED slot

or an audio trigger can ask where the water is without a C++ module.

The node catalogue is built by walking MClassRegistry, so every MFUNCTION here
becomes a node on its own — nothing is hand-registered.

members.doc:
Everything at once, then read out. A footstep or an ambience wants four of
the answers above at the same point, and each of those calls walks every

types.name: FActorSpawnTransform
types.doc:
The pose a spawn verb asked for, applied during registration so it is in
place before OnConstruct and BeginPlay run: a graph that reads its own
location from its first event must see where it was put, not the origin.
Each field is optional so a location-only spawn leaves a root component's
authored rotation and scale alone. Rotation is Euler radians, the
TransformComponent's own storage, so a rootless actor reads back exactly
the triple it was spawned with instead of a quaternion round trip.

types.name: MWorld
types.doc:
MWorld is a GC root: the mark phase reaches every spawned actor
through the MPROPERTY m_actors list (and from there components via
the actors' own MPROPERTY fields). An actor's Outer pointing at the
world does NOT keep the actor alive — only the m_actors edge does.

members.name: SpawnActor
members.signature: template<typename T, typename... Args> TWeakObjectPtr<T> SpawnActor(Args&&... args)
members.doc:
Spawning
Construct + register an actor in this world. The world becomes
the actor's outer; BeginPlay fires (or is queued if tick is
mid-frame). Returns a TWeakObjectPtr so callers can detect
post-GC sweep — DON'T store as raw AActor*.

members.name: SpawnActorByClass
members.signature: AActor* SpawnActorByClass(MClass* cls, const std::function<void(AActor*)>& preRegister = {}, const FActorSpawnTransform* initialTransform = nullptr)
members.doc:
Spawn by runtime class (hot-reload restore, scene-deserialized
actors). Returns nullptr when cls is null, lacks a codegen
factory, or isn't an AActor subclass. `preRegister` runs after
construction (default subobjects exist) but BEFORE RegisterActor —
restore property values there so the ECS mirror publishes them.
`initialTransform` is applied during registration, ahead of OnConstruct
and BeginPlay: onto the root component when the actor has one, else
onto the backing TransformComponent the moment it exists.

members.name: SpawnActorFromTemplate
members.signature: AActor* SpawnActorFromTemplate(FName templateName, const std::function<void(AActor*)>& preRegister = {}, const FActorSpawnTransform* initialTransform = nullptr)
members.doc:
Spawn an instance of a registered template (archetype instancing). The
instance derives its defaults from the template rather than the class
CDO and remembers the template's name, so the scene writer diffs it
against the template. Returns nullptr when the template is not
registered in FActorTemplateRegistry.

members.name: InitializeGameMode
members.signature: AGameMode* InitializeGameMode(MClass* gameModeClass = nullptr, bool spawnLocalPlayer = true)
members.doc:
Game framework
Spawn the game mode (cls, or base AGameMode when null), call
InitGame + StartMatch. One per world; repeated calls return the
existing mode. Typically invoked by the runtime after the start
scene loads, with the class named in project settings.
spawnLocalPlayer false = dedicated server: no local PlayerController
or default pawn; connections get pawns through AGameMode::RestartPlayer.

members.name: BeginPlay
members.doc:
Registration and play are separate transitions. Registering an
actor publishes its ECS mirror — that is what makes a placed actor
visible and inspectable in the editor, and it happens at scene
load. BeginPlay fans out only here, when the host enters play
(Scene::OnRuntimeStart / OnSimulationStart).

Both are idempotent and each actor begins play at most once per
play session: an actor spawned mid-play begins play during its
registration and is skipped by a later world BeginPlay, and a
Play → Stop → Play cycle re-runs BeginPlay exactly once per cycle.

members.name: Tick
members.doc:
Lifecycle
Whole-frame tick: BeginTickFrame, all four groups in order, then
SyncActorTransforms. Correct only when nothing needs to run BETWEEN
groups — a host that steps physics mid-frame drives the pieces below
instead (Scene::OnUpdateRuntime does exactly that, so PostPhysics
actors observe post-physics poses).

Begins play first when it has not begun. This path is a game path
by construction — an editor host drives the pieces below and calls
BeginPlay itself — so a headless driver that only ticks still gets
the lifecycle it expects rather than silently unplayed actors.

members.name: BeginTickFrame
members.doc:
The frame-ordered pieces of Tick, so the caller can interleave a
physics step. Call order per frame: BeginTickFrame → TickGroup
(PrePhysics) → TickGroup(DuringPhysics) → SyncActorTransforms(false) →
physics → TickGroup(PostPhysics) → TickGroup(PostUpdateWork) →
SyncActorTransforms(true).

BeginTickFrame advances the frame stamp the prerequisite resolver
dedups against — exactly once per frame, never per group.

members.name: GetTimerManager
members.doc:
World-scoped timers (UE parity): set here, a timer dies WITH the
world — it can never fire into a torn-down actor the way an
engine-scope FTimerManager::Get() timer can. Ticked at the start of
the PrePhysics group, so it pauses when the world stops ticking.

members.name: GetTimeSeconds
members.doc:
Time (UWorld parity). All of it reads the process frame clock in
Core — a world does not own a clock, it presents one — so the
numbers agree with FTime, FApp and every other module that asks.
Defined out of line so a caller in another DLL resolves them here
rather than inlining its own read.

members.name: TimeSince
members.doc:
Game seconds since a stamp taken from GetTimeSeconds(). Does not
advance while paused.

members.name: GetEffectiveTimeDilation
members.doc:
The dilation actually applied to this frame's tick delta: zero
while paused.

members.name: SetWorldPaused
members.doc:
Per-WORLD pause/dilation — a second axis on top of the process-global
FTime clock the methods above mirror (TimeTests pins that mirroring).
This axis lets two worlds differ: a paused PIE world under a live
editor world, a slow-motion cutscene world beside a real-time UI
world. Applied inside TickGroup, so both MWorld::Tick and hosts that
drive TickGroup directly (Scene::OnUpdateRuntime) honour it; a paused
world fires no timers and ticks no actors.

members.name: SyncActorTransforms
members.doc:
Push each actor's root world transform into its backing entity.
`onlyChanged` writes only actors whose root moved since the previous
sync this frame — which is what lets the post-physics sync land
PostPhysics actor movement WITHOUT clobbering the poses physics just
wrote for actors that did not move themselves.

members.name: Destroy
members.doc: Despawn an actor: calls EndPlay, removes it from the list, deletes it.

members.name: NotifyBackingEntityDestroyed
members.doc:
The scene deleted an entity out from under its actor (outliner
delete): tear the actor down too, without re-entering the entity
destruction hooks. No-op for plain entities.

members.name: GetActors
members.doc:
Removal leaves a null hole so it costs no search and no shift; the
holes are squeezed out here and once a frame by the tick schedule, so
a caller never sees one.

members.name: InvalidateTickLists
members.doc:
The tick schedule is rebuilt once a frame from canEverTick,
primaryTickGroup and the components' tickGroupOverride, which are plain
fields. A mid-frame change that takes an actor OUT of a group applies at
once (dispatch re-checks the fields); one that puts it INTO a group
still to run this frame needs this call, or it lands next frame.
Spawning, destroying and AddComponent invalidate on their own.

members.name: NotifyActorComponentAdded
members.doc:
AActor::AddComponent reports here so a component added mid-frame with a
tickGroupOverride still ticks in this frame's pass, as it did when every
pass walked the whole actor list.

members.name: FindActorByEntity
members.doc:
Resolve the actor backing an ECS entity, or nullptr when the
entity is plain ECS data (or its actor is pending kill). This is
the address translation the networking layer needs: replication,
relevancy and RPC routing all key off the entity carrying
NetworkObjectComponent, and this is what turns one of those ids
back into the gameplay object that owns it.

members.name: GetECSWorld

types.name: FPlatformOverlayPolicy
types.doc:
What the game does while the platform overlay is up. Ducking and muting are
separate flags because in a game whose audio carries the threat, silence is
information the overlay was never meant to hand the player — so ducking is
the default and a full mute is an explicit choice.

types.name: FPlatformOverlay
types.doc:
Applies that policy to the online-service seam's overlay notification.

Every effect goes through an injected hook. The pause target is not the same
object in a packaged runtime and in a PIE session, and the part that can
actually be wrong is the state machine — it has to survive a repeated open,
a close with no matching open, and a close after the player paused the game
themselves, without ever restoring state the game has since taken over.

members.name: Install
members.doc:
Binds the handler to FOnlineServices and installs the default hooks
(FTime pause, InputManager cursor, AudioEngine master volume) for any
hook the host has not already replaced. Safe with no platform up: the
seam's default is a no-op and nothing ever fires.

members.name: SetMultiplayerQuery
members.doc:
True while the session has remote peers. A networked world keeps
running with the overlay up — the other players are still in it and
there is no pause to hand them.

members.name: OnOverlayActivated
members.doc:
The transition. Idempotent per edge: a second `true` changes nothing,
and a `false` with no open before it restores nothing.

members.name: DidPauseWorld
members.doc:
What the handler is currently holding, so a host (and the self-test)
can tell an overlay-driven pause from a game-driven one.

members.name: Reset
members.doc:
Drops every hook and clears the held state without restoring it —
for a test that wants a clean handler, and for a host tearing its
world down under an open overlay.

members.name: PredictActivateAbility
members.doc:
Client-side prediction
On a client the player owns no authority, but waiting a full round-trip
before the cost/cooldown/cue land feels laggy. These predict an
activation LOCALLY the instant the input arrives, and reconcile against
the server's verdict: a confirm keeps the local result, a reject rolls
every touched attribute + tag + effect back to the captured pre-activation
baseline. The server stays authoritative — a predicted activation never
changes anything the server does not also do.

PredictActivateAbility captures the baseline, runs the local activation,
and returns a non-zero prediction key when it applied (0 = the local
CanActivate check failed, so nothing was predicted and there is nothing to
reconcile). Works for both lambda-spec and class-based abilities.

members.name: ConfirmPrediction
members.doc:
Server confirmed the prediction: drop the retained baseline (the local
result stands; replicated attributes converge it to the exact value).

members.name: RollbackPrediction
members.doc:
Server rejected the prediction: restore the captured baseline and drop
the record. A stale/unknown key is a no-op.

types.name: FGameplayCueDispatcher
types.doc:
Process-wide, data-driven cue dispatch. HandleCue routes a fired cue to the
most specific installed handler whose tag is an ancestor-or-equal of the
cue tag (so a handler on "GameplayCue" catches everything under it, while a
handler on "GameplayCue.Death" overrides it for that subtree), then to the
observer. A cue with no matching handler is a silent no-op — the authored
data survives even when nothing is wired to play it.

Install a handler for a cue-tag subtree. Re-registering the same tag

members.doc: Sees every fired cue regardless of tag — runs after the subtree handler.

members.doc:

members.name: CueWireId
members.doc:
A cue that crosses the wire travels as a 32-bit id, never as an FName
index (those are per-process) and never as a string (the RPC codec takes
fixed-width parameters only). The id is FNV-1a32 of the tag PATH — the
same construction as MAbilitySystemComponent::AbilityWireId, so the two
read alike in a packet dump.

Resolving an id back to a tag needs the receiver to have SEEN the tag.
Unlike an ability id — which the receiver can look up in the replicated
granted set — a cue has no such list, so the registry is populated from
everything that names a cue tag locally: installing a handler for a
subtree, and firing a cue. A game with authored cue tags nothing has
touched yet registers them explicitly.

types.name: FGeometricAcousticsSystem
types.doc:
The scene's geometric acoustics. On its first tick it builds the acoustic
geometry — its own scan hierarchy over the level when the ScanHierarchy
plugin is loaded, else the physics scene — and installs the scan hierarchy
for the world, which moves every occlusion query (world sources, proximity
voice, radio, AI hearing) onto the scanned walls. Then, a few times a
second, it re-traces the space around the listener: the decay and the
absorption the walls really have go to the echo tail, and the exact early
reflections replace its per-distance guess in the reverb impulse response.

Echolocation: Echolocate sends a click out of a cone, reports the echoes,
tells the AI a click was heard, and plays each returning echo from where it
bounced once its round trip has elapsed (audio.Acoustics.EchoClip).

types.name: FInteractionDelegates
types.doc:
Broadcast synchronously when a pawn interacts with an actor — AFTER the
interactable's own reaction, BEFORE the Visual Script OnInteract pins (the order
the old direct QuestSystem call had). Consumers (quest objectives,
analytics) resolve their system through the world at call time instead
of the InteractionSystem naming them, so they can live in plugins.

Deliberately NOT the EventBus: DispatchImmediate runs handlers under the
bus mutex, and an interact handler can cascade into Visual Script graphs that
post events — a self-deadlock. This is a plain game-thread multicast
with captureless handlers (registration order = call order; never register
per-world state). A handler lives as long as the module whose code it is:
unloading that module removes it.

types.name: FHairAsset
types.doc:
A groom: guide curves in the asset's own space, read from a .mhair MDF file

Hair "Ponytail" {
schema_version: 1
strands_per_guide: 24      // interpolated render strands per guide
root_width: 0.004          // ribbon width at the root, world units
tip_width: 0.001
clump_radius: 0.012        // spread of a guide's children at the root
clumping: 0.35             // how far children pull back to their guide toward the tip
Guide { points: [vec3(0, 1.7, 0), vec3(0, 1.65, -0.02), ...] }

Every guide is resampled to kPointsPerStrand points evenly along its length
on load, so the simulation and the GPU ribbon expansion work on one fixed
layout. BuildChildren then scatters the render strands: each child sits at
a jittered root around its guide and follows the inverse-distance blend of
the three nearest guides' shapes, pulled toward its own guide by Clumping.

types.name: FRemoteConfig
types.doc:
FRemoteConfig — values a live game can change without a patch: defaults in
code (or a defaults file), overridden by a signed document fetched over

variant. A document only applies when it verifies against the project's
signing key and is not older than the one in force, so neither a tampered
response nor a replayed old one can change the game.

A/B: a user's variant of an experiment is a pure function of the user id
and the experiment name (FNV-1a into 10 000 buckets, walked against the
variant weights), the same on every launch and every machine; reading a
variant records one "experiment_exposure" telemetry event per experiment.

types.name: EMeshColliderSource
types.doc:
Where the collider a fresh placement gets came from. Reported so the caller
(and the test) can tell an artist's authored setup from a shape the engine
measured, which are the two answers that must never be confused: one is a
decision, the other is a stand-in for a decision nobody made yet.

members.name: HasFittedFallback
members.doc:
The box the mesh's own bounds fit, carried even when Source is Authored.
This is the mark: a collider equal to it is one this helper measured and
nobody has touched since, so a mesh that GAINS an authored setup after
placement can replace its stand-in without ever overwriting a human's
numbers. Nothing is stored on the component — being recomputable from the
mesh is what makes the mark survive a save/load round trip.

types.name: FMeshColliderDefaults
types.doc:
What collider a freshly placed mesh should get. Nothing in the engine used
to create one at all: every instantiation site added a MeshRenderer and
stopped, so a placed prop either had no collision or — once a human added a
Collider and left the enum alone — collided as a half-metre box regardless of
what it looked like. UE's contract is the one implemented here: a placed
static mesh collides by its mesh's own collision setup, and a mesh with no
setup gets a primitive fitted to it rather than a fixed default.

This decides and writes component fields only. Cooking stays in the Physics
image, where Jolt's per-image allocator is armed — nothing here allocates a
Jolt shape.

r.Physics.AutoCollider, and therefore also the project's

types.name: FLidarGpuTrace
types.doc:
The scale path for the trace. A grenade is thousands of rays in one frame,
which is a dispatch, not a loop of physics queries — but it is the SAME
pattern the CPU trace walks, so a shot fired here and a shot re-traced on a
client that fell back to the CPU produce the same cloud.

Output is a dense record per ray rather than an atomically appended list:
the index is the ray index, so the buffer is reproducible and a hit can be
matched back to the ray that found it.

members.name: IsSupported
members.doc:
True when the device can run the trace at all. Needs inline ray query for
the traversal and 64-bit ints for the vertex fetch that resolves normals.

members.doc:
Records the dispatch into the current command buffer. `instanceData` is

members.name: ReadBack
members.signature: uint32_t ReadBack(const FLidarShot& shot, std::vector<HitRecord>& outRecords)
members.doc:

members.name: ResolveHits
members.signature: static uint32_t ResolveHits(const HitRecord* records, uint32_t count, const ESurfaceType* instanceSurfaces, uint32_t surfaceCount, const uint8_t* instanceDynamic, std::vector<FLidarHit>& outHits)
members.doc:
Turns raw records into hits, resolving each point's colour from the
surface of the instance the ray landed on. `instanceSurfaces` and
`instanceDynamic` are indexed by TLAS instance id — the renderer's
GetRaySceneSurfaces / GetRaySceneDynamicFlags hand them over directly
for a live-scene trace. A short table degrades to Default rather than
reading out of bounds.

members.name: maxPoints
members.doc: The whole point budget of this machine's view of the world.

members.name: sharedShare
members.doc:
The share of it other players' scans may fill (the audit's C5: 20%).
A client never holds anyone else's cloud; it re-traces the shots it
receives, and this is how many of their points it keeps.

types.name: FLidarScanService
types.doc:
The scan loop between a scanner and the clouds. Every machine holds its
OWN cloud (what this player scanned, owner slot 0) and a SHARED cloud
(what the others scanned, re-traced locally from their shots, tinted by a
per-player slot 1..7) — and nothing else: there is no global cloud on any
machine, the host included. Shots, not points, cross the network: a shot
fired in a session goes out through FNetSession::ReportLidarShot, which
applies it here at once and relays it to everyone, whose services re-trace
it into their shared cloud.

members.name: Attach
members.signature: void Attach(Scene& scene, const FLidarScanConfig& config, TraceFn trace)
members.doc:
Finds or creates the two cloud entities ("ScanCloud.Own" and
"ScanCloud.Shared") and takes over the session's shot delegate.

members.name: Fire
members.doc:
A shot from this machine's player. In a session it is reported and
comes back through ApplyNetShot; outside one it is applied directly.

members.name: ApplyNetShot
members.doc:
A shot the session delivered: this player's own (the local echo) goes
to the own cloud, anyone else's to the shared cloud under their slot.

members.name: OwnerSlotFor
members.doc:
Stable per session: the first other player seen gets slot 1, the next
2, and so on round to 7. Player ids are never reused and run past 7,
so the slot is a mapping, not the id.

members.name: Tick
members.doc:
Advances every Fill wave still spreading, releasing the hits the front
has reached. The scanner system calls it every frame.

scanner system asks before every shot. No gate = every scanner fires.

types.name: ELidarPattern
types.doc:
How a shot distributes its rays. Every scanner variant in the game is one of
these plus numbers — a wide sweep, a tight long-range beam and a grenade that
floods a room differ only in cone width, ray count, range and falloff, so
"gun variants" stay content rather than code.

types.name: FLidarShot
types.doc:
One trigger pull, and the entire replication payload for it. A shot is
re-traceable from these bytes alone: every ray direction is a pure function
of (seed, tick, rayIndex) and the shot's frame, with no RNG state carried
between rays and no dependence on frame rate or on how many shots came
before. Sending this instead of the resulting points is the difference
between tens of bytes and megabytes per trigger pull.

members.name: densityFalloff
members.doc:
>1 concentrates rays toward the axis (a tight dot in the middle, sparse
at the rim); 1 spreads them uniformly over the cap. This is the knob that
separates a focused scanner from a floodlight without changing ray count.

members.name: rangeBand
members.doc:
The scanner's range band (1 far, 2 normal, 3 precise; 0 none): the
points it makes carry it, and it picks their dedup grid.

members.name: waveSpeed
members.doc:
A Fill's reveal speed in metres per second, 0 for a shot that lands at
once. A Fill paints a whole room; landing it in one frame is a flash,
so its hits are released outward from the origin at this speed.

members.name: dynamic
members.doc:
Points that landed on something that can move are never admitted to the
persistent cloud — they belong in the ephemeral set that decays, which is
also the horror beat: scan, see a silhouette, scan again, it is gone.

members.name: response
members.doc:
What the scan-response table did to this hit, and how long the caller
should sit on it. Both stay at their defaults on every trace with no
table installed, which is every caller that existed before the table.

types.name: FLidarPattern
types.doc:
The deterministic ray pattern, and the single definition of it. LidarTrace.comp.hlsl
mirrors these four functions instruction for instruction; the GPU trace and
the CPU trace must agree or a client re-tracing a replicated shot draws a
different cloud than the shooter did.

members.name: Basis
members.signature: static void Basis(const Vec3& dir, Vec3& outTangent, Vec3& outBitangent)
members.doc:
Deterministic orthonormal basis around `dir` — a pure function of the
direction, so two machines given the same shot build the same frame.

members.name: Direction
members.signature: static Vec3 Direction(const FLidarShot& shot, uint32_t rayIndex)

members.name: TraceCPU
members.signature: static uint32_t TraceCPU(PhysicsWorld& world, const FLidarShot& shot, std::vector<FLidarHit>& outHits)
members.doc:
Traces the shot against the physics world on the CPU. Deterministic and
side-effect free: it reads the physics broadphase and writes `outHits`,
so the same shot against the same world state always produces the same
hits in the same order. Appends; it does not clear `outHits`.

members.name: TraceCPU
members.signature: static uint32_t TraceCPU(PhysicsWorld& world, const FLidarShot& shot, const FQueryFilter& filter, FTraceBatch& batch, std::vector<FLidarHit>& outHits)
members.doc:
Batched form. `batch` is the caller's ray storage — hold one per scanner
and a shot allocates nothing after the first — and `filter` is where the
shooter's own capsule goes, now that a character has an inner body a ray
starting inside it would otherwise report at zero distance. Determinism
is unaffected: results are written per ray index, so the parallel and
serial paths produce the same hits in the same order.

members.name: TraceCPU
members.signature: static uint32_t TraceCPU(PhysicsWorld& world, const FLidarShot& shot, const FQueryFilter& filter, FTraceBatch& batch, const FScanResponseTable* responses, uint64_t seed, std::vector<FLidarHit>& outHits)
members.doc:
The same trace with the scan-response table in the loop. A null table is
the passthrough the two overloads above forward through, so a caller
that installs no table runs the identical code and gets the identical
cloud — the responses are an addition to this path, not a fork of it.

The table keys on the hit's surface type as its tag and on the hit
entity as its instance, so a creature installs a rule on itself without
inventing a material. Penetrate re-casts through PhysicsWorld::QueryRay;
every other response is resolved in place.

types.name: FPointCloudBudget
types.doc:
What happens when the cloud is full, stated as data rather than left to a
clamp somewhere. Pages are the resource that actually runs out: the GPU pool
is `maxPoints / kPageCapacity` pages and a chunk holds one page per
kPageCapacity of its points, so a sparse chunk costs one page and eviction
frees a predictable amount.

members.name: quantizeStep
members.doc:
Dedup grid. Two rays that land within this distance of each other on the
same surface produce one point, which is what stops a player standing
still and holding the trigger from eating the whole budget. It also
absorbs last-ulp differences between two machines re-tracing one shot.

members.name: rangeQuantizeSteps
members.doc:
The dedup grid per scanner range band (the record's 3-bit range): a far
scan keeps one point per 8 cm, a normal one per 4 cm, a precise one per
1.5 cm. 0 falls back to quantizeStep, which is what band 0 — a cloud
that never sets a range — uses. Bands never dedup against each other,
so a precise pass adds detail over a far one instead of being eaten by it.

members.name: minRankCeiling
members.doc:
Decimation floor — a chunk is never thinned below 1/16 of its density.
Past that the cloud stops reading as a surface and eviction is honest.

members.name: ephemeralCapacity
members.doc:
The decaying half. Its points share the component's SSBO but sit PAST the
last page, in the space PointCloudComponent::ephemeralCapacity allocated
on top of maxPoints — carving them out of the page pool would shrink the
persistent budget of every cloud that already exists. 0 drops dynamic
hits.

types.name: FPointCloudChunk
types.doc:
Points are ordered by a rank that is a pure function of the dedup cell they
occupy, so "draw at half density" is "draw the first half" and "thin this
chunk" is "drop the tail" — both stable under insertion order, which is what
lets a decimated chunk survive a save/load round-trip unchanged. The chunk's
points are split across pages in that order: page k holds points
[k * kPageCapacity, (k + 1) * kPageCapacity), so thinning frees pages off the
end and a distance LOD is a prefix of the first few.

members.name: newestBirth
members.doc:
The newest birth stamp in the chunk, kept on insert and on a re-scan's
re-stamp, so the 1 Hz expiry pass asks one number per chunk.

members.name: dedupSlots
members.doc:
Only exists between the first insert after a sort and the next sort. A
chunk nobody is scanning needs no lookup table, and at a full budget the
table held for every resident chunk cost half as much again as the points.

members.name: chunksExpired
members.doc: Chunks whose every point had fully faded, dropped by the 1 Hz pass.

types.name: FPointCloudMemory
types.doc:
Where the bytes go, measured rather than estimated: capacities, not sizes, so
vector slack and a dedup table left behind both show up.

types.name: FPointCloudAccumulator
types.doc:
The persistent half of a scanned world: every point that landed on something
that cannot move, held chunked by sector so it can be culled, thinned,
evicted and written to disk a piece at a time.

members.name: AddHits
members.signature: uint32_t AddHits(const FLidarHit* hits, uint32_t count, uint64_t tick, const Vec3& viewerPosition, uint8_t owner = 0, uint8_t rangeBand = 0)
members.doc:
Admits a trace's hits and splits them: static ones join the persistent
chunks, dynamic ones go to the owned ephemeral ring, which decays them.
One sink rather than two because the caller has one list and splitting it
at every call site is how the dynamic half ends up dropped — which is
exactly what happened: the ring was written, tested, and never fed.
Returns the number of STATIC points admitted.
`owner` is the tint slot the points carry (0 = this player's own scan,
1..7 = the others', as the renderer reads it).

members.name: AddPoints
members.signature: uint32_t AddPoints(const FPointCloudSample* samples, uint32_t count, uint64_t tick, const Vec3& viewerPosition)

members.name: AddScanPoints
members.signature: uint32_t AddScanPoints(const FScanPoint* points, uint32_t count, bool dynamic, uint64_t tick, const Vec3& viewerPosition)
members.doc:
The Embree scan hierarchy's output. It carries no motion type, so the
caller says whether the pulse hit something that can move.

members.name: SetGpuStore
members.doc:
The GPU point store mode (r.PointCloud.GpuStore): the persistent cloud
lives in a GPU hash table that inserts, dedups and fades it there, and
this accumulator only forwards the new static samples — no CPU chunk,
dedup table or page is touched. The ephemeral ring stays here. Points
held before the switch keep drawing from their pages.

members.name: TakeGpuPending
members.doc: Hands over every sample forwarded since the last call.

members.name: GetGpuForwarded
members.doc: Total forwarded samples, for the cost readout.

members.name: Flush
members.doc:
Orders every touched chunk by rank and refreshes its LOD prefix table.
Cheap and idempotent; AddHits leaves chunks unsorted so a burst pays one
counting sort per chunk instead of one per point.

members.name: CollectVisible
members.signature: void CollectVisible(const FPointCloudView& view, std::vector<FPointCloudDrawRange>& outRanges) const

members.name: GpuBufferPoints
members.signature: static uint32_t GpuBufferPoints(uint32_t maxPoints, uint32_t ephemeralCapacity)
members.doc:
The buffer a component needs for a cloud of `maxPoints` plus its ring:
the page pool rounded down to whole pages (never below one) and the
ring on top.

members.name: kEphemeralTicksPerSecond
members.doc:
The ephemeral half's clock. It is deliberately NOT the shot tick: a shot
tick is part of the shot's identity (two machines re-tracing it must get
the same rays) and it only advances while somebody is firing, whereas a
silhouette has to keep fading after the trigger is released. Advance it
from the frame clock at a fixed rate so the fade is the same length on
every machine.

members.name: AdvanceAllEphemerals
members.signature: static void AdvanceAllEphemerals(World& world, float deltaSeconds)
members.doc:
Advances every cloud in the world. The fade has to keep running on a
scene tick and not on a draw, because a scene drawn twice in one frame
(an editor viewport beside a PIE view, split screen) would otherwise age
its points twice as fast as a scene drawn once.

members.name: kMaxFadeSeconds
members.doc:
The PERSISTENT half's fade clock. A scanned surface that never dims
turns a scanner game into a lighting pass done once, so a point carries
the moment it was revealed and the shader derives its remaining life
from that — no per-frame CPU decay and no re-upload, which is the only
way this stays affordable at millions of points.

The stamp is a u16 of kBirthTicksPerSecond ticks. A point dark for
longer than the longest fade a cloud can author is clamped to exactly
that age by the expiry sweep, long before its stamp could wrap round
and read as freshly scanned.

members.name: kMinEphemeralLifetimeTicks
members.doc: 350 ms at the ephemeral ring's 60 Hz: the shortest fade-out allowed.

members.name: kBirthClampTicks
members.signature: static constexpr uint32_t kBirthClampTicks = static_cast<uint32_t>(kMaxFadeSeconds * FPointCloudLayout::kBirthTicksPerSecond)

members.name: AdvanceAge
members.doc: fadeSeconds <= 0 turns ageing off and nothing is stamped.

members.name: AdvanceAllAges
members.signature: static void AdvanceAllAges(World& world, float deltaSeconds)

members.name: LifeOfBirth
members.doc:
The remaining life the shader will compute for a stamp, for tests and
for gameplay that wants to know whether a sector has gone dark.

members.name: MakePersistentStyle
members.doc:
Draw style for the persistent half: the component's authored splat and
fade rows plus this accumulator's live fade clock.

members.name: GetEphemeralFirstPoint
members.doc:
First point of the region the ring writes: immediately past the last
page, i.e. exactly where the component's extra ephemeral capacity
begins.

members.name: ExtractChunksInRect
members.signature: uint32_t ExtractChunksInRect(float minX, float minZ, float maxX, float maxZ, std::vector<FPointCloudChunk>& outChunks)
members.doc:
World streaming's half of the cloud. A sector that streams out hands its
chunks to FSectorCloudResidency, which parks them and hands them back on
load; the extract releases the GPU pages and the point memory with them.
Membership is by the chunk's sector CENTRE, so a chunk on a cell boundary
belongs to exactly one cell and a park and a restore cannot both claim it.

members.name: AdoptChunks
members.doc:
Takes as many chunks as the page pool has room for and leaves the rest in
`chunks` — a caller that ignores the remainder is dropping player-scanned
points, which is why they are handed back rather than silently discarded.
Points landing on a sector that was scanned again while it was parked go

members.name: SaveToMemory
members.doc:
A scanned world is far too big to live in the component's MDF node, so it
persists as its own chunk stream — zstd over a flat record per sector.
Records are stored exactly as the GPU reads them, page aside, so a
round-trip is bit-exact and a reloaded cloud accepts exactly the same
new points that the original would have.

The file's budget does not travel: a cloud loads into the budget this
accumulator already has, thinned densest-chunk-first if it does not fit.
Taking the writer's budget is how a component sized for two million
points was quietly regrown to the eight million some older save named.

Float math whose result is the same bit pattern on every machine the game
ships to. The C runtime's sin/cos/pow are free to differ in the last ulp
between MSVC, glibc and Apple's libm, and one ulp in a ray direction moves a
far hit by a point's width — enough for two clients re-tracing the same
replicated shot to draw different clouds. These use only +, -, *, / and
sqrt, which IEEE 754 rounds exactly, in a translation unit compiled with FMA
contraction off.

types.name: FScanBvh
types.doc:
The deterministic scan hierarchy (§29 A2). Shots replicate, not points, so
every client re-traces every shot — and the cloud a player sees is only
shared if every client's trace returns the same hits bit for bit. Jolt and
Embree cannot promise that: they are float hierarchies built in an order
that follows the ECS iteration and the thread schedule, and the two of them
do not even generate the same rays.

This one is canonical by construction:
- vertices are snapped to a 1/1024 m grid as they are added, so every
coordinate is exactly representable and the build never sees two
machines' transform round-off;
- triangles are sorted by a content key (Morton code of the snapped
centroid, then the snapped vertices, then the tag), so the hierarchy is
the same whatever order the level's meshes were added in;
- traversal reports the nearest hit with ties broken by that canonical
triangle index, so neither child order nor thread count changes a result;
- a shot's rays are cast in parallel but written per ray index.

Static geometry is built once; moving bodies go into a second hierarchy
rebuilt each Sync from their current transforms, deterministic as long as
the transforms themselves are the replicated state.

types.name: FFixed
types.doc:
Q16.16 fixed point for gameplay state that must come out the same bits on
every machine and every build: the float rules a compiler may follow
(contraction into FMA, x87 vs SSE, reassociation under fast-math) differ
across toolchains, and integer arithmetic does not. Products and quotients
widen to 64 bits before they narrow, and both round toward negative
infinity, so the result never depends on the sign convention of a division.

Inside one binary, strict IEEE float (the engine builds /fp:precise) is
already deterministic; FFixed is for state that crosses builds — a replay,
a dedicated server on another platform.

types.name: FRewindBuffer
types.doc:
FRewindBuffer — time rewind as a gameplay feature: a ring of saved states,
one every 1/captureHz seconds, holding the last `seconds` of play within a
memory budget, any of which can be made the present again. It saves and
restores through the same IRollbackGame a rollback session uses, so a
world that rolls back rewinds, physics state included.

A rewind lands on a captured moment, not between two: the newest capture
at least as old as asked, or the oldest one when the buffer holds less.
That capture stays in the buffer, so rewinding again goes further back.

not anything in the message — and a message that claims another sender is
dropped.

types.name: FRollbackSession
types.doc:
FRollbackSession — GGPO-style rollback for any number of players over any
transport. Each frame the local input is filed `inputDelay` frames ahead
and sent; inputs not yet heard from a peer are predicted (its last known
input repeated); the frame is simulated at once. When a peer's real input
for an already-simulated frame differs from what was predicted, the state
saved before that frame is restored and every frame since resimulated with
what is now known. Peers that fall more than `maxPrediction` frames behind
stall the local simulation instead of predicting further.

Desync detection: once every player's input for a frame is confirmed, the
state saved at that frame is final; every `checksumInterval` frames each
peer sends that state's checksum, and a mismatch is reported (OnDesync) —
the moment two machines stopped agreeing, not the moment it became visible.

types.name: FRollbackSystem

switch on and an online session running, every player is a rollback player
in player-id order; the scene's ECS world becomes the rollback simulation,
advanced at net.Rollback.TickRate with the steps games register
(RegisterStep), each player's input written into its RollbackPlayer
component every frame. Session messages ride the online session's events
(the host relays between clients). Offline, a one-player session runs the
same fixed-step loop, so a game behaves the same alone and online.

The physics scene is not part of the scene rollback: PhysicsSystem steps
on wall-clock time and owns its bodies' lifetimes. Physics that must roll
back belongs to a physics world the game steps inside a registered step —
FRollbackWorld covers it when one is handed in.

types.name: SaveGameManager
types.doc:
Owns save slots on disk plus a migration registry so titles that ship
updates can promote old saves without breaking compatibility.

File layout (per slot):
{save_dir}/slot_{NN}.mwsave           — MDF document, see SaveGame.cpp
{save_dir}/slot_{NN}.png              — optional screenshot
{save_dir}/slot_{NN}_cloud_{E}_g{G}.mpcl — one scanned point cloud per
owning entity and save generation,
see below

`save_dir` defaults to FPaths::UserSaveGamesDir() —
<Product>/Saved/SaveGames under the per-user state root. A packaged game
writes there directly; the editor/PIE adds a per-project subfolder under
the engine root. Apps with multiple branches or per-user-profile saves
can override via SetSaveDirOverride().

members.name: kPointCloudSchema
members.doc:
Schema of the slot's `PointClouds` block. A scanned world is millions
of points — orders of magnitude past what belongs inside the save
document — so each cloud is written as its own `.mpcl` sidecar and the
document records only the entity → file mapping. Without it a save
slot restores the world with everything the player revealed erased,
which in a scanner game is the whole save.

Every save writes its sidecars under a fresh generation and records the
generation and each sidecar's CRC in the document. Overwriting one set of
names in place let a crash, a failed async write or a fall back to `.bak`
pair a document with another save's clouds. A sidecar is deleted only
after the new document is renamed into place, and only when neither it
nor the backup names it and no newer save still waiting to land wrote it.

members.name: kJournalSchema
members.doc:
Layout versions of the engine-owned blocks of a world-state slot. The
root `schema_version` is the game's (SetCurrentSchema); these move only
with the engine, so a game bump and an engine change cannot be confused.

members.name: FWorldAuthorityFn
members.doc:
Co-op: the world belongs to whoever is authoritative for it. A client
that autosaved its replicated copy of the host's world, or loaded one,
diverged from the host the moment it did — so SaveWorldState and
LoadWorldState refuse off-authority, whatever called them (autosave,
travel, a checkpoint, a Visual Script graph). Personal progress belongs in a
progress object (SaveGameObject), which every player keeps. The default
answer is "not a client of a net session"; a game with other rules
(a dedicated server's own policy) installs a provider.

members.name: SaveSlot
members.signature: bool SaveSlot(uint32_t slot, Scene* scene, const SaveData& custom, const SaveSlotMetadata& metadata, const std::vector<uint8_t>& screenshotPNG = {})
members.doc:
DEPRECATED for games: kept for tools and the tests that pin its format.
It writes the whole scene into the slot, so LoadSlot replaces the level
with the one the save was taken on and a patched level loses to an old
save. A game saves the world with SaveWorldState (a delta over the
packaged level) and its progress with SaveGameObject.

Snapshot the scene + custom data + metadata into slot N. Returns
false on I/O failure. metadata.slotIndex / timestampUnix /
schemaVersion are filled by the manager — callers only supply the
designer-facing fields (playerName, sceneName, playTimeSeconds).

`screenshotPNG`, if non-empty, gets written as a sidecar file
`slot_NN.png` next to the .mwsave. The caller is responsible for
capturing + encoding (we deliberately don't pull the renderer into
the SaveGame module — runtime games + editor have different
capture paths).

types.name: FMeshRenderProxyCache
types.doc:
The game-thread half of the persistent render scene: one proxy per entity
that draws through a MeshRenderer, holding what the mesh gather used to look
up again for every entity on every view — five hashed component lookups and
the collider's surface type, which for a collider naming a .mphysmat is a
mutex-guarded cache lookup.

The list is rebuilt only when the world's signature version moves. Every
create, destroy, AddComponent, RemoveComponent, snapshot restore and world
reset bumps it, and those are the only operations that move component
storage, so a pointer taken under one version stays valid until the version
changes. Field edits need no rebuild because the proxy reads the components
live; the one derived value, the surface type, is re-resolved only when the
collider's own fields or the physics-material cache generation change.

The proxy never holds a mesh or a material. Those are read through the
MeshRenderer each frame, so an in-place asset hot reload that frees and
replaces a mesh's internals can never leave a proxy pointing at the old one.

members.name: Sync
members.doc: Brings the proxies in line with the world; true when the list was rebuilt.

members.doc:

members.doc:
The signature version the proxies were built under. A caller walking the

members.name: Invalidate

types.name: FModelInstantiator
types.doc:
Turns an imported model's source node graph into an actor/entity tree, the
UE analogue of dragging an FBX with several mesh objects: a model whose
nodes carry more than one geometry object expands into a parent + one child
entity per node (each with its own TransformComponent and a
MeshRendererComponent bound to that node's submeshes), instead of collapsing
everything onto a single flat entity. Single-mesh and skinned models keep
the single-entity representation. Pure CPU — no GPU objects are touched, so
the same builder backs both the editor drop path and the headless tests.

members.name: GeometryNodeCount
members.doc: Number of nodes in the tree that carry geometry (non-empty meshIndices).

members.name: ShouldInstantiateHierarchy
members.doc:
A model earns a hierarchy when it has a real node tree with more than one
geometry-bearing node and is NOT skinned (a skinned mesh stays one entity
carrying the skeletal mesh + skeleton, never one entity per bone).

members.name: BuildHierarchy
members.signature: static int32_t BuildHierarchy(Scene& scene, EntityID rootEntity, const std::string& modelPath, const std::vector<ModelNode>& nodes)
members.doc:
Build one child entity per node under `rootEntity`, preserving the source
parent links (root nodes attach to `rootEntity`). Geometry nodes receive a
MeshRendererComponent bound to `modelPath` with modelNodeIndex set so the
resolver pulls only that node's submeshes; every node receives a
TransformComponent decomposed from its local transform. gpuMesh is left
unresolved (the scene's hydration pass fills it, same as a flat drop).
Returns the number of entities created.

members.signature: static void AssignNode(MeshRendererComponent& mrc, const Ref<MeshAsset>& asset, int32_t nodeIndex)
members.doc:
Resolve a single node's submeshes onto `mrc`, at identity local
transforms (the node's placement lives in the entity's TransformComponent
+ parent chain, so baking it here would double-apply it). Used by the
scene-hydration / runtime resolvers when a MeshRenderer carries a
modelNodeIndex >= 0. No-op when the asset or node index is invalid.

types.name: PrefabInstantiator
types.doc:
Engine-side prefab → entity-tree instantiation. Operates on
PrefabAsset (already parsed MDF nodes per entity) so it works in
Runtime / dedicated server / any build without the editor.

What's deserialized (scope):
Transform, Light, RigidBody, Collider, AudioSource, AnimatorComponent,
Camera, ParticleEmitter, ...
Limitation: MeshRenderer / Material asset resolution is handled
best-effort via AssetManager::TryGet() — works for assets present in
the runtime's MEAF mount but not for hot-loaded editor assets; the
editor keeps its own instantiation path for that reason.

The Replication framework calls this on the client to materialize a
ghost entity when it receives a Spawn packet referencing a prefab.

members.signature: static Entity Instantiate(const Ref<PrefabAsset>& prefab, Scene* scene, const Vec3& position = Vec3(0, 0, 0), const Vec3& rotation = Vec3(0, 0, 0))

members.doc:

members.name: ReapplyPrefab
members.signature: static bool ReapplyPrefab(const Ref<PrefabAsset>& prefab, Scene* scene, EntityID rootId)
members.doc:
Prefab live-link: rebuild a placed instance from `prefab` (its
source), then replay the instance's stored per-component overrides.
This is the "propagate a prefab edit to instances" path — after the
prefab file changes, every instance re-derives its components from
the new source while local overrides survive on top. `rootId` is an
instance root (Scene::GetEntityPrefabSource set); the operation walks
rootId + descendants that share the same source path and lines each
one up with its source entry via Scene::GetEntityPrefabSourceIndex.
Entity identity, hierarchy and outside references are preserved (the
rebuild is in-place, not a destroy+respawn). Returns false if rootId
isn't an instance. Nested-prefab subtrees (a different source path)
are left alone — propagate their own prefab separately.

members.doc:

members.name: CapturePrefabOverride
members.signature: void CapturePrefabOverride(EntityID id, const std::string& componentDisplayName)
members.doc:

instance as an override — a CDO-delta MDF blob (only properties that

members.name: EvaluateVolumes
members.doc:
Volume framework

EvaluateVolumes is the per-frame hook that walks the scene's
VolumeComponents, blends their profiles using `cameraPos`, and writes
the result back into `m_environment.postProcess` so the existing
SceneRenderer read path picks it up unchanged.

Baseline handling: on the first call after scene load (or after a
PostProcessBaseline reset) the current `m_environment.postProcess` is
captured as the authored baseline. Subsequent frames blend volumes
on top of that baseline. To edit the baseline live, disable all
volumes (or call `InvalidateVolumeBaseline`) so the next evaluation
captures the inspector's fresh values.

members.name: InvalidateVolumeBaseline
members.doc:

the next EvaluateVolumes call. Editor's Volume inspector triggers

physics mirror (bodies + character controllers, velocities kept) by

when the main camera drifts past wp.RebaseDistance (snapped to
wp.RebaseGrid). The accumulated offset maps rebased coordinates
back to absolute world space: absolute = local + offset.

members.name: GetNavData
members.doc:
Navigation mesh (baked per scene). Null until a bake is done or a
pre-baked .navmesh is loaded. NavAgentSystem reads this each tick
to plan paths; with no nav mesh it falls back to straight-line
steering (Scope A behavior).
Opaque: the baked nav asset type lives in the AINavigation plugin,
which loads the companion .navmesh on scene attach and pushes it
into its nav systems (FNavMeshProvider in the plugin wraps the cast
for typed callers). Core stores only the owning reference so scene
lifetime keeps the bake alive.

members.name: SetFocusHighlightProvider
members.doc:
Focus-highlight provider (plugin seam): the interaction system used
to be named here directly; now whoever owns "what entity should the
renderer highlight" registers a captureless provider. Process-wide.

members.name: FindUnboundPlacedNetworkEntity
members.signature: static EntityID FindUnboundPlacedNetworkEntity(World& world, const char* prefabPath, const Vec3& position, uint64_t placedGuid)
members.doc:
Replication seam: the scene-placed entity a client-side Spawn packet
should ADOPT instead of materializing a fresh ghost. Server and client
load the same scene file, so a placed NetworkObject already exists in
the client's world when its Spawn arrives — spawning a ghost on top of
it is the placed-object double-spawn.

`placedGuid` is the authored identity off the Spawn packet and settles
the match on its own when both sides have it. It is 0 for a runtime
spawn, a pre-v4 sender, or a scene saved before the stamp existed, and
then the match falls back to what shipped before: the authored prefab
path plus the nearest pose among still-unbound candidates — which pairs
interchangeable twins wrongly once they have moved. Anything already
bound to a NetworkId or spawned by a previous packet is never
considered. INVALID_ENTITY = no candidate (dynamic spawn — the caller
materializes a ghost as before).

members.name: AssignPlacedNetworkGuids
members.doc:
Stamp a stable identity on every scene-placed NetworkObject that lacks
one, and break any collision an old copy-paste left behind. Returns how
many entities were changed. Called from the save path so authoring an
object is all a designer has to do; exposed because a scene assembled in
code (tests, a generator) needs the same guarantee before it is hosted.

members.name: ReleaseAdoptedPlacedNetworkEntities
members.doc:
Hand every scene-placed NetworkObject back to the scene when a session
ends. `networkId` and `spawnedRemotely` are session state written onto an
entity the SCENE owns, and nothing else clears them, so a placed twin a
join adopted stays marked as somebody's ghost forever. The next join then
skips it in FindUnboundPlacedNetworkEntity and materializes a second copy
— the double-spawn adoption exists to prevent, returning through leave →
rejoin. Runtime-spawned ghosts are left alone: they belong to the session,
not the scene, and the reload path already discards them. Returns how many
entities were released.

members.name: GetOrCreatePointCloudAccumulator
members.signature: FPointCloudAccumulator* GetOrCreatePointCloudAccumulator(EntityID id, const FPointCloudBudget& budget)
members.doc:
Scanned point clouds. The Scene owns the accumulator behind every
PointCloudComponent (keyed by entity), exactly so the save path has an
owner to flush: SaveToFile writes each cloud's .mpcl companion and
records its path on the component before the scene is serialized, and
LoadFromFile rebuilds the accumulator from that path — the same shape
as the terrain flush and the nav-mesh companion. Game code asks the
scene for the accumulator instead of owning one; the component's
runtime pointer is a non-owning view of the scene-owned object.

The save path restores clouds from slot-owned sidecars rather than from

over the scene's shipped scan, and two slots of the same level have to
hold two different revealed worlds.

untouched. Returns the number of entities successfully merged (0 if

members.doc:

and a Relationship sub-node when parented inside the tree. The
*outer* parent of the root is intentionally not encoded; callers

members.signature: EntityID RestoreEntityTreeFromMdf(const std::string& mdfStr, const FWorldStateJournal* skipJournal = nullptr)

games, replication ghosts, sibling Constraints — keep resolving),
restores their components, and rewires parent links within the
tree. Returns the root entity id on success or INVALID_ENTITY on
parse/restore failure. Existing entities with colliding UUIDs are
skipped — undo never silently merges over a live entity.

members.signature: static std::unordered_map<std::string, std::string> RemapCopiedTrees(const std::vector<MDF::MdfNode*>& trees)
members.doc:
Copy/paste and duplicate of a SET of trees (each an `EntityTree` node
from SerializeEntityTreeToNode): one remap across the whole set, so
every entity gets a fresh uuid and every parent link and actor or
component reference naming another member of the set follows it to the
copy. Pasting the trees one by one gave each its own remap, and a copy
kept pointing at the original of anything copied beside it. Returns
old uuid string -> new.

members.name: SerializePrefabFromEntities
members.signature: std::string SerializePrefabFromEntities(const std::vector<EntityID>& roots, const std::string& prefabName, std::unordered_map<EntityID, int32_t>* outIndices = nullptr, const std::string& selfSourcePath = {}) const
members.doc:
Author a `.mdfprefab` document from a live actor selection: every given
root plus its descendants is written as index/parent_index Entity nodes
carrying their reflected components, in the container shape PrefabAsset
loads and PrefabInstantiator instantiates. A single selected root becomes
the prefab root; multiple roots are collected under a synthesized group
entity at the origin so the result is always single-rooted. Returns the
MDF text (empty on failure). outIndices (optional) receives the entry
index assigned to each serialized entity — the caller that overwrites
an existing .mdfprefab needs it to restamp the instance's
prefabSourceIndex values so a later propagation pairs entities with
the right entries (the serializer numbers entries fresh each time).
selfSourcePath: the prefab file this serialization will overwrite.
Instantiated members are stamped with their source path, so without it
an instance's own children read as nested instances and get written as
`nested_prefab` references to the very file being rewritten — the
instantiator's cycle guard then refuses them and the applied prefab
silently loses every child. Pass empty when authoring a NEW prefab
(a stamped child there is a genuinely foreign nested instance).

types.name: SceneSnapshot
types.doc:
Compressed in-memory snapshot of a Scene's serialized state.

Used by PIE (edit → play state capture). The compressed buffer is owned
by the SceneSnapshot — copy/move semantics are explicit so call sites
stay obvious about lifetime.

Storage model:
- Capture takes the Scene's serialized MDF text, re-encodes it to the
compact mdfb binary form, then runs zstd on the binary and stores
the compressed bytes — smaller than zstd(text) and cheaper to parse
back on restore.
- Restore decompresses into a temporary std::string holding the mdfb
bytes; MdfDocument::ParseFromString auto-detects the MDFB magic, so
Scene::DeserializeFromMDF consumes it unchanged (and old text
snapshots would still parse).

This is intentionally not a full delta journal — the roadmap calls for
per-mutation journaling for an additional ~20× win, but the immediate
short-term goal is "stop holding the raw MDF string for the entire PIE
session." Compression + immediate release accomplishes that.

types.name: FMeshAssetResidency
types.doc:
Residency of the mesh assets a host loaded for its scene follows the entities
that use them, as a World Partition cell's packages do in UE: when a sector
streams out, its entities drop their references, and an asset nothing but the
host's share-by-path cache still holds is released. Before this the cache kept
every mesh that had ever streamed in until the next travel, so the CPU and GPU
memory of a long session tended toward the whole world's unique meshes.

members.name: TakeUnreferenced
members.signature: static std::vector<Ref<MeshAsset>> TakeUnreferenced(std::vector<Ref<MeshAsset>>& cache, const std::function<bool(const MeshAsset&)>& heldByAssetManager = nullptr)

them back, so the caller can drop what it bound to them before the last
reference goes. `heldByAssetManager` says which assets the asset manager
also caches — one more reference that is not a user; the manager's own
LRU sweep frees those. Null entries are dropped too.

members.name: memoryBudgetBytes

Ceiling on the asset bytes resident sectors may hold, from the sizes the
cook stamped into the manifest. 0 = no ceiling, which is what every
build had: the three radii are a DISTANCE budget, and on a map whose
sectors are heavier than the machine they were tuned for, distance alone
is how a level fits in memory on one machine and does not on another.
Over the ceiling, the load queue stops at the sector that would cross it
— nearest first, so the ones a player is about to reach still win — and
an already-resident sector is never evicted for it.

types.name: FStreamingSectorCookJob

its collision twin, which is where the time goes on a big level — and

cook abandoned after any number of steps leaves the old one intact. The
editor drives this from its tick under a progress card; the one-shot
BuildManifest below is the same three calls back to back.

types.name: FTextureStreamer
types.doc:
Texture mip-streaming (slice 1). A streamable texture is a cooked
.mtex whose per-mip table lets us read ANY mip range without touching
the rest of the file. Registration makes only the coarse TAIL resident;
StreamTo(mip) re-reads mips [mip..N) and swaps in a new image (Vulkan
commits an image's full memory at creation, so residency changes are
recreate-and-swap — the UE non-virtual streaming model). Synchronous
v1; async via StreamingIOQueue and GPU-copy reuse of already-resident
levels are follow-ups. Consumers must re-query GetImage() after a
stream (the Ref changes) — cached descriptor sets keep the OLD image
alive until rebound.

members.name: Register

members.doc:

members.doc:

members.name: StreamTo
members.doc:

Returns false when the handle/mip is invalid or IO fails (previous

members.signature: bool StreamToAsync(uint32_t handle, uint32_t topMip, IOPriority priority = IOPriority::High)

happen on the main thread). A newer request for the same handle
supersedes a pending one (the stale read's apply is dropped).

types.name: FVramPressureGovernor
types.doc:
Turns the driver's VRAM budget into a cap on a streaming pool (one governor
per pool: textures, mesh LODs). The configured pool is a guess made at
startup (half the card); the budget the OS grants shrinks when another
process takes VRAM, and a pool that keeps asking for its full size past that
point pages the whole process out of local memory. Over the high mark the cap
drops to the resident streaming bytes minus this pool's share of the
overshoot, so the farthest textures or least recently seen meshes coarsen
first; under the low mark it relaxes by a quarter of the headroom per update
and lifts entirely once it no longer constrains anything. Pools that share
one budget split the overshoot by their resident bytes (SharedOvershoot):
each taking the whole of it would evict twice what the budget needs.

members.name: kFloorBytes

types.name: FTerrainEditLayer
types.doc:
One non-destructive sculpt layer. `delta` is the layer's contribution in
meters and `coverage` records where the layer has authored anything at all —
Alpha/Min/Max need to tell "authored 0" from "never touched", which a bare
delta grid cannot express.

types.name: FTerrainEditLayerStack
types.doc:
The stack behind every height edit. Ops still run on a plain composited
FEditableHeightfield — nothing downstream (mesh build, collision, GPU
upload) knows layers exist — but the difference an op made is folded into
the ACTIVE layer, so hiding that layer restores the terrain underneath it
exactly instead of leaving a baked-in dent.

members.name: SetBase
members.doc:
Replaces the unlayered floor without disturbing the stack — an import,
a procedural regenerate or an offline erosion pass writes here.

members.name: BeginOp
members.signature: void BeginOp(const FEditableHeightfield& composite, const FTerrainTexelRegion& region)
members.doc:
Op capture. BeginOp snapshots the composite over the window the op is
about to touch; EndOp folds (after - before) into the active layer and
re-composites, so the field the caller holds always equals
base + visible layers and never drifts from it.

members.name: EndOp
members.signature: bool EndOp(FEditableHeightfield& composite, const FTerrainTexelRegion& region)

members.name: Composite
members.signature: void Composite(FEditableHeightfield& out, const FTerrainTexelRegion& region) const
members.doc: Recomputes `out` from base + visible layers over `region` (empty = all).

members.name: CollapseToBase
members.doc:
Drops every layer's contribution into the base and empties the stack —
the "Flatten Layers" command.

members.name: kSerializedVersion
members.doc:
Persistence. The stack is what makes a sculpt non-destructive, so a scene
that stores only the composite heightmap has already thrown the authoring
away — the whole stack, BASE INCLUDED, goes into one blob so a reload can
recompute composite == base + visible layers instead of trusting the
flattened file it also wrote. Planes are raw little-endian float32 and
uint8: exactness beats size here, because a quantized delta would drift
the composite away from the heightmap saved next to it.

types.name: FTerrainHydraulicParams
types.doc:
Droplet-based hydraulic erosion. Offline by design: a full pass over a
1025² field is seconds of CPU, so it belongs behind an explicit "Erode"
button, not on a brush dab.

types.name: FTerrainThermalParams
types.doc:
Talus-angle relaxation: material above the repose angle slides downhill.
This is what turns noise cliffs into scree slopes.

members.name: talusJitter
members.doc:
Per-texel variation of the repose angle, as a fraction of the talus
height. A uniform angle relaxes a cone into a perfect four-sided
pyramid, because the 4-neighbour stencil is symmetric and nothing ever
breaks the tie; real scree does not do that. The jitter is derived from
the seed and the texel coordinate rather than drawn from a stream, so
the pass stays a pure function of (field, params) and repeats exactly.

types.name: FTerrainErosionRun
types.doc:
How far a pass run a slice at a time has got. Stepping one to the end leaves
the field exactly as one full call does: the droplet stream and the
per-iteration jitter both carry on from here.

members.signature: static FTerrainTexelRegion Hydraulic(FEditableHeightfield& field, float worldSize, const FTerrainHydraulicParams& params)

Both run in place over the whole field and return its full extent, so
the caller uploads/rebuilds once instead of chasing per-droplet rects.

can spread seconds of CPU over frames and stop between slices. Both

Chunk grid for one tile: the coarsest split whose chunk resolution stays

exactly. An inexact split leaves the last chunk row short, which shows up

`tileWorldSize` apart — anything else double-counts the overlap and
leaves a seam the stitcher cannot close.

types.name: FTerrainNoiseAsset
types.doc:
FTerrainNoiseAsset (.mnoise) — an authored procedural noise stack, the thing
UE5 has no equivalent of: World Machine's layer list as a first-class asset.
It stores the LAYERS, not a baked heightfield, so the same stack drives a
whole-field generate on a 1025² terrain, a brush pattern that keeps its grain
at any radius, and a 128² preview thumbnail from one description.

The stack is deliberately resolution-independent — every frequency is cycles
per METER — which is what lets a stack authored against a 256 m terrain be
dropped on a 4 km one and still read as the same landscape.

members.name: baseHeight
members.doc:
The value every blend starts from, so a Multiply-only or Min-only stack
still has something to act on.

members.name: previewWorldSize
members.doc:
The world span the PREVIEW is rendered over. Not a property of the
stack — the stack is scale-free — but a preview needs some window, and
storing it means reopening the asset shows the framing it was authored
against instead of an arbitrary default.

members.name: RenderPreview
members.signature: void RenderPreview(uint32_t size, std::vector<uint8_t>& outGray) const
members.doc:
Grayscale preview, `size` x `size`, row-major, normalized so the lowest
sample is 0 and the highest 255. Empty when the stack evaluates flat —
a flat stack has no contrast to stretch and any normalization would
amplify float noise into visible banding.

members.name: PreviewRange
members.signature: void PreviewRange(uint32_t size, float& outMin, float& outMax) const
members.doc:
Min/max of the stack over the preview window, in meters. The panel shows
it because amplitude is the one stack property a normalized preview
deliberately hides.

types.name: FTerrainOffsetField
types.doc:
Per-texel XZ displacement of the render grid, in meters — UE5's landscape
XY-offset map. The heightfield stays a regular grid; this says where each of
its samples actually SITS in the world, which is the whole trick behind
Retopologize: a cliff sampled on a regular XZ lattice spends almost all its
triangles on the flat ground above and below it and almost none on the face,
because uniform XZ spacing is non-uniform 3D spacing the moment the surface
tilts. Sliding samples toward the steep parts spends the same triangle budget
where the silhouette is.

Heights are never rewritten. A displaced sample's height is the field
sampled AT the displaced position, so the surface is unchanged and only the
tessellation moves along it — that is what makes the tool non-destructive and
what the tests measure.

members.name: GetOffsetX
members.signature: float GetOffsetX(uint32_t x, uint32_t y) const
members.doc:
Zero for any out-of-range texel, so a caller never has to bounds-check
before asking where a sample went.

members.name: GetOffsetZ
members.signature: float GetOffsetZ(uint32_t x, uint32_t y) const

members.name: SetOffset
members.signature: void SetOffset(uint32_t x, uint32_t y, float offsetX, float offsetZ)

members.name: MaxMagnitude
members.doc:
Largest |offset| in the field, in meters. Zero means the grid is still
regular and nothing downstream has to consider offsets at all.

members.name: maxOffsetTexels
members.doc:
How far a sample may leave its lattice position, as a fraction of the
texel spacing. Past ~0.5 neighbouring samples can cross and the mesh
folds, so the op clamps to it.

members.name: strength
members.doc:
Fraction of the computed correction applied per iteration. One pass at
full strength overshoots on a cliff edge and oscillates.

members.name: slopeThreshold
members.doc:
Below this 3D-slope (rise over run) a texel is left alone. Flat ground
is already uniformly tessellated and moving it only smears the
weightmap-to-geometry correspondence for nothing.

members.name: SamplePosition
members.signature: static void SamplePosition(const FTerrainOffsetField& offsets, uint32_t x, uint32_t y, uint32_t width, uint32_t height, float worldSize, float& outX, float& outZ)
members.doc: Where texel (x,y) actually sits, in terrain-local meters.

members.name: SampleDisplacedHeight
members.signature: static float SampleDisplacedHeight(const FEditableHeightfield& field, const FTerrainOffsetField& offsets, uint32_t x, uint32_t y, float worldSize)
members.doc:
The height the DISPLACED sample renders at: the unchanged field, sampled
at the displaced position. This is the function the "heights are
preserved" test measures — the surface must be the same surface.

members.name: Relax
members.signature: static FTerrainTexelRegion Relax(const FEditableHeightfield& field, FTerrainOffsetField& offsets, const FTerrainRetopoParams& params)
members.doc:
Relaxes the whole field toward uniform 3D spacing. Returns the touched
window (the whole grid) so the caller uploads once.

members.name: RelaxStamp
members.signature: static FTerrainTexelRegion RelaxStamp(const FEditableHeightfield& field, FTerrainOffsetField& offsets, const FTerrainBrushStamp& stamp, const FTerrainRetopoParams& params)
members.doc:
Brush form: the same relaxation weighted by the dab's radial falloff, so
an artist retopologizes the one cliff they are looking at instead of the
whole landscape. Returns the touched texel window.

members.name: SpacingUniformity
members.signature: static double SpacingUniformity(const FEditableHeightfield& field, const FTerrainOffsetField& offsets, float worldSize)
members.doc:
Mean 3D distance between horizontally adjacent samples divided by its own
standard deviation's complement — the uniformity probe the tests measure
against. Higher is more uniform; a retopologize pass that works raises it.

types.doc: One evaluated point of the resampled centreline, in terrain-local meters.

members.name: raise
members.doc:
A road cut into a hillside must be allowed to remove material but not to
build a causeway across the valley below it — the two directions are
separately switchable for exactly that reason.

types.name: FTerrainSpline
types.doc:
Landscape splines: a polyline with a per-point width profile that flattens
the heightfield into a corridor and paints a layer along it. Pure geometry —
it never touches the component, the GPU or the collider, so the same call
serves the editor, a procedural road generator and the tests.

members.name: Resample
members.signature: static std::vector<FTerrainSplineSample> Resample(const std::vector<FTerrainSplinePoint>& points, int32_t segmentsPerSpan)
members.doc:
Catmull-Rom through every control point, `segmentsPerSpan` samples per
span. Fewer than two points resamples to nothing.

members.name: ClosestOnCenterline
members.signature: static bool ClosestOnCenterline(const std::vector<FTerrainSplineSample>& samples, float worldX, float worldZ, FTerrainSplineSample& outSample, float& outDistance)
members.doc:
Nearest point on the resampled polyline, with the profile interpolated
along the segment. Returns false when there is no centreline.

members.name: InsertIndexFor
members.signature: static int32_t InsertIndexFor(const std::vector<FTerrainSplinePoint>& points, float worldX, float worldZ)
members.doc:
Where a shift-click at (worldX, worldZ) belongs in the control array.
A road is refined mid-span far more often than it is extended, so the
answer is the nearest SPAN's far index — appending everything would fold
the corridor back on itself the first time an author clicks behind the
last point. Beyond either end it extends instead.

members.name: TangentAt
members.signature: static Vec3 TangentAt(const std::vector<FTerrainSplinePoint>& points, int32_t index)
members.doc:
The tangent a point contributes to the centreline: its authored one when
it has one, otherwise the Catmull-Rom tangent the curve already implies —
which is what lets a tangent handle start ON the curve instead of
snapping it straight the moment it is grabbed.

Creates a paintable weightmap when the component references none, seeded
from the procedural slope/height rules so the first stroke blends into
what is already on screen instead of snapping the whole terrain to one
layer. Idempotent; returns false when the terrain has no splat material.

members.name: GetWeightmapPixelData
members.signature: uint8_t* GetWeightmapPixelData(EntityID entity, uint32_t& outWidth, uint32_t& outHeight)
members.doc:
Mutable view of the CPU weightmap the GPU texture mirrors — the paint
brush writes here and follows with UploadWeightmapRegion over the same
rect. Null when the entity has no weightmap.

members.name: EnsureEditableHeights
members.doc:
Sculpt session
The editable float grid backing height edits. Built lazily from the
component's heightmap at whatever precision the source carries, or flat
when it references none. Once present it becomes the authority: a
fingerprint rebuild composes the mesh from it, not from the file.

members.name: SetEditableHeights
members.signature: bool SetEditableHeights(EntityID entity, const FEditableHeightfield& field)
members.doc:
Installs a field wholesale — a tiled import cutting one oversized source
into a grid, or a generator. The layer stack is dropped with it: deltas
authored against the old grid cannot be recomposited onto a new one, and
keeping them would shift every stroke by a row. Clears the component's
fingerprint so the next Update rebuilds mesh, collision and CDLOD data at
whatever resolution the new field carries.

members.name: AdoptUnsavedEdits
members.doc:
Takes the live edit state of a world this one was copied from — sculpted
heights, painted weightmaps, retopo offsets — for every entity that
exists here too (a play-in-editor copy keeps the source's entity IDs).
A sculpt lives here and not in the scene document until the level is
saved, so without it a copy rebuilt every terrain from the files on disk
and PIE played on the last saved landscape. Call before the copy's first
Update so its first build composes from the adopted field. Returns how
many terrains took edited heights.

members.name: RebuildHeightRegion
members.signature: uint32_t RebuildHeightRegion(EntityID entity, const FTerrainTexelRegion& region)
members.doc:
Rebuilds only the chunks whose texel footprint intersects `region`
(an empty region rebuilds every chunk). Returns how many chunks were
rebuilt — the measurement the brush stroke cost is dominated by.

members.name: RefreshCollision
members.doc:
Resamples the Jolt heightfield from the edited grid. Separate from the
mesh rebuild because it invalidates the physics body; call it once at
stroke end, not per dab.

members.name: SaveHeightsToFile
members.signature: bool SaveHeightsToFile(EntityID entity, const std::string& absPath, float heightScale) const
members.doc:
Persistence
Heights write as headerless little-endian 16-bit (the .r16 the decoder
already reads back at full precision), normalized against heightScale.
The weightmap writes as an RGBA8 PNG. Both take an absolute path; the
caller sets the component's VFS path to match.

members.doc:
Largest edited height, for choosing a heightScale that does not clip the
sculpt on save. Returns 0 when the entity has no edit session.

members.name: AcceptFingerprint
members.doc:
Marks the component's current field values as already built, so writing
freshly saved heightmap/weightmap paths back into it does not trigger a
full rebuild of geometry that is already correct.

members.name: ApplySculptStamp
members.signature: FTerrainOpResult ApplySculptStamp(EntityID entity, const FTerrainBrushStamp& stamp)
members.doc:
The seam a viewport tool calls. The stamp's world XZ is TERRAIN-LOCAL
meters (origin at the terrain centre); `worldSize` on the stamp's brush
is overwritten from the component, so a tool never has to know it. The
op routes through the active edit layer, then refreshes the CDLOD height
texture and quadtree bounds for the touched rect only. Collision is NOT
refreshed — that costs a physics-body rebuild, so call EndStroke once
when the drag releases.

members.name: ApplyPaintStamp
members.signature: FTerrainOpResult ApplyPaintStamp(EntityID entity, const FTerrainBrushStamp& stamp, int32_t layer)
members.doc:
Paints one layer (negative = erase toward a hole) and pushes the dirty
rect to the GPU weightmap, which is what invalidates the RVT pages.

members.doc:
Offline whole-field passes. Each is one explicit command, not a dab:
they rewrite the field, rebuild every chunk and refit collision once.

members.doc:
The same passes a slice at a time, for the editor to spread over frames.
Every slice redraws the chunks; collision is refit once, by the slice
that finishes the run, because refitting it every frame of a long pass
